summary: CNBC reports that military experts and defense analysts see little chance of a Ukrainian breakthrough in 2024 after the 2023 counteroffensive failed to meet expectations. Fighting is expected to continue as attritional battles, with Russia consolidating gains in the east and Ukraine on the defensive. The war's course will largely depend on U.S. aid and the outcome of the U.S. presidential election, and negotiations remain unlikely.
one_line: Analysts told CNBC that Ukraine is unlikely to achieve a breakthrough in 2024, with the war's course hinging heavily on U.S. aid and the election.
key_facts: Military experts and defense analysts told CNBC that a Ukrainian breakthrough in 2024 is unlikely and that Kyiv's forces are unlikely to launch more counteroffensives.
The much-vaunted Ukrainian counteroffensive expected in spring 2023 did not change the course of the war; Ukrainian military officials conceded expectations of a great breakthrough were not met.
Ukrainian forces struggled to break through heavily fortified Russian positions along a roughly 600-mile-long front line and liberated only a handful of villages in the summer.

Ukraine's attacks on Russian bases and assets in Crimea this summer prompted the Russian navy to withdraw a number of warships from Sevastopol, which Kyiv counts as a victory in the battle of the Black Sea.
Intense fighting continues around Bakhmut and Avdiivka, where Russian forces are conducting offensive operations and have made some confirmed advances despite deteriorating weather.
The Institute for the Study of War said Russia is likely pushing offensives to seize the initiative before the Russian presidential elections in March 2024.
A senior Ukrainian army general warned that front-line troops face artillery shortages and have scaled back some operations because of a shortfall of foreign assistance.
Retired Army Lt. Gen. Stephen Twitty warned that if Ukraine is not resupplied and re-funded, the war could tilt to the Russians; otherwise a stalemate and future frozen conflict is possible.
Sam Cranny-Evans of RUSI said Ukraine is significantly more reliant on the U.S. than on the EU, and that EU ammunition production is far below where it should be.
Former U.S. Ambassador to NATO Kurt Volker expects U.S. and EU aid packages to be approved in January, tiding Ukraine over for another year, and wants longer-range missiles and Western aircraft.
F-16 jets have been pledged by Norway, Denmark and the Netherlands; Ukrainian pilots are starting training, but deployment could take months, and the U.S. is not providing its own F-16s.
Donald Trump, the Republican front-runner, says he could end the war 'in one day' if reelected; Volker doubts Trump would abandon Ukraine but says future funding would be uncertain.

Zelenskyy said the military asked for up to 500,000 additional conscripts but he needs to hear 'more arguments'; Ukraine's Defense Ministry says its main 2024 goal is boosting its domestic defense industry.
Mario Bikarski of the Economist Intelligence Unit said that a Republican win and substantially reduced funding would increase pressure on Ukraine to negotiate.
